reading.body:
Maryland's 2026 legislative session treated data centers as a utility problem, not just a land-use one. Of 104 bills, the ones naming data centers directly concern siting, operation standards, county property tax subclasses, rate schedules for large load customers, and a proposed moratorium on new construction.

That cluster is the tell. Bills like SB1000 on certificates of public convenience, SB992 and HB940 on large load customer registration and demand response, and HB1082 on data center rate schedules all reach the same question: who pays for the power and the interconnection when a single customer draws at that scale. HB120 goes furthest, pairing a construction moratorium with co-location and generation contingency language. HB560 would repeal sales, use, and property tax exemptions for data centers, and HB1595 and SB427 would let counties tax their personal property separately. The legislature is working the cost-allocation seam, not the compute seam.

The rest of the docket is consumer and civil law aimed at AI outputs rather than AI infrastructure. Chatbot liability, companion chatbot regulation, AI in behavioral health and health insurance, algorithmic rent setting, deepfake identity fraud, and an algorithmic addiction fund all appear, several in both chambers. Education bills on AI guidelines and a Maryland AI Partnership sit alongside them. None of this touches model training, chips, or interconnection queues.

What the data does not show is outcome. These are bill records with dates, not enacted law, and the list carries no vote counts, fiscal notes, or effective dates. It also cannot say how much load Maryland data centers actually draw, or whether any of these measures passed. The pattern is legislative attention, and attention is not the same as constraint.

The bill list is dominated by pairs. SB168 and HB810 carry the identical blockchain title, SB238 and HB340 the identical school psychologist compact, SB141 and HB145 the identical deepfake election title, SB8 and HB184 the identical identity fraud title. Maryland's legislature works by cross-filing, so a title appearing twice is a signal of sponsorship intent rather than two separate policies. The practical consequence is that counting bills overstates the breadth of the agenda. The 104 records collapse into a smaller number of distinct proposals, and the data centers cluster is smaller still once duplicates are removed.

The energy bills split into two functions that are easy to conflate. One set governs how a large load connects: SB596, HB940, SB992, and HB1082 all address interconnection, registration, or rate schedules for large load customers. A second set governs who captures the tax base: HB1595, SB427, HB560, and HB1411 address county property tax subclasses, exemption repeal, and planning transparency. The first is about the grid operator's relationship with a single customer. The second is about the county's relationship with the same customer. Both are cost-allocation fights, but they sit in different committees and different levels of government.

The dates run in one direction. The earliest bills in the list are from January 13, 2026, and the latest from May 30, 2026, which is consistent with a single session's introduction and crossover calendar rather than a multi-year record. The news items sit later still, from September and October 2026, and they are about a governor's framework and a bipartisan governors group, not about the bills. The data cannot connect the two: nothing in it says which bills became law or which the framework drew on.

What did Maryland actually pass on data centers in 2026?
The data does not hold this. It lists bill numbers, titles, and dates, with no vote counts, signatures, or effective dates, so passage cannot be determined from it.

Why do so many bills appear twice with different numbers?
Maryland cross-files legislation, so a Senate bill and a House bill with the same title are companion versions of one proposal. SB168 and HB810, SB238 and HB340, and SB141 and HB145 are examples in this list.

Which Maryland bills would directly raise the cost of building a data center?
HB120 would impose a moratorium on new data center construction with co-location and generation contingency language. HB560 would repeal sales, use, and property tax exemptions for data centers, and HB1534 would set standards for their operation and siting.

Does Maryland tax data centers differently from other commercial property?
The data shows bills that would change the answer, not the current rule. HB1595 and SB427 would let counties establish a subclass and set a special personal property rate for data centers, and HB560 would repeal existing exemptions.

How much electricity do Maryland data centers actually consume?
The data does not contain load figures. It names large load customers as a category in SB596, HB940, SB992, and HB1082 but gives no megawatt or consumption numbers.

What does the Maryland AI Partnership bill do?
SB597 establishes a higher education Maryland Artificial Intelligence Partnership. The data gives the title and date only, with no funding level, scope, or institutional participants.
